extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of U.S. state constitutional law and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive textbook account of the powers, offices, procedures, and institutions of U.S. state executives and judiciaries, suitable for understanding or evaluating state constitutional arrangements and administrative practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veto power of the governor
rubrics_metrics.description: He has in all the States but one (North Carolina) a veto upon bills passed by the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This veto may be overridden in the manner already indicated, but generally kills the measure because if the bill is bad it calls public attention to it, and if unobjectionable the governor's veto is probably party-motivated; the use of the veto is a governor's most serious duty and chiefly by his discharge of it is he judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to ensure faithful administration of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: He is charged with the duty of seeing that the laws of the State are faithfully administered by all officials and the judgments of the courts carried out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes the governor's obligation to require information from other executive officials and to communicate to the legislature his views regarding the condition of the commonwealth; policy largely rests with the legislature whose statutes may prescribe executive action tightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning and reprieving powers
rubrics_metrics.description: In nearly all States the governor has the power of reprieving and pardoning offenders, but in some this does not extend to treason or to conviction on impeachment (in Vermont he cannot pardon for murder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some recent Constitutions impose restrictions evidencing distrust of the prerogative; the power has sometimes been used to release offenders (e.g. against the election laws) who deserved no sympathy; in some States other authorities are associated with the governor in exercising this prerogative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander-in-chief role and militia powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The governor is commander-in-chief of the armed forces of the State, can embody the militia, repel invasion, suppress insurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The militia are chiefly used to suppress riots (often connected with labour disputes); some States have created small State police forces (e.g., Massachusetts' District Police, Pennsylvania State police, Michigan's State police for anti-liquor enforcement, New York's for supervising elections, Delaware has detectives) placing them at the governor's disposal for maintenance of order and enforcement of administrative regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment powers and confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: He appoints some few officials, but seldom to high posts, and in many States his nominations require the approval of the State Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State patronage is of slight value because many important offices are directly elected; nevertheless there is a tendency to commit to the governor selection of capable men for posts recently created, often subject to confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to require information and convey views to legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: He has the right of requiring information from the other executive officials, and is usually bound to communicate to the legislature his views regarding the condition of the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He may recommend measures and practically cause bills embodying his recommendations to be introduced; in a few States he is directed to present estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor's role as public leader and measure of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of his veto and his discharge of executive duties chiefly determine how the governor is judged by the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong and upright governor can become a post of effective leadership, represent the people's will, and at times be supported against the legislature; the office affords opportunity for display of character and talents and can be a stepping stone to higher office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lieutenant-governor functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The elective Lieutenant-Governor who, in most States, steps into the governor's place if it becomes vacant, is usually also ex officio President of the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Otherwise he is often an insignificant personage, though sometimes a member of executive boards; where there is no lieutenant-governor, succession is usually by President of the Senate or Secretary of State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive council or cabinet variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some States have councils or cabinets (e.g., Massachusetts' executive council, Florida's 'cabinet of administrative officers', North Carolina's council) which advise the governor and may have powers such as rejecting nominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such bodies are survivals of older arrangements that may lessen the governor's responsibility but can be helpful; their membership and method of selection vary (elected or appointed) and can act as an administrative check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied names and duties of other state officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The names and duties of other officers vary from State to State: most frequent are secretary of state, treasurer, attorney-general, comptroller, auditor, superintendent of public instruction; occasionally state engineer, surveyor, superintendent of prisons, and various boards for railroads, canals, prisons, agriculture, labour, immigration, public utilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many officials are elected at the general State election, sometimes chosen by the legislature or appointed by the governor (often with Senate confirmation); salaries and term lengths vary (rarely exceed four years; examples such as New Jersey and Tennessee exceptions are given); textbooks provide concrete examples (Ohio list with duties and salaries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Election vs. appointment of officials and terms
rubrics_metrics.description: State officials are often elected by the people, though some are chosen by the legislature or appointed by the governor; terms and salaries vary with office and State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher officials chosen by the people are elected for short terms on party lines; in some States appointments and term lengths are conservative outliers (e.g., NJ secreatary/attorney-general five years; TN attorney-general eight years appointed by supreme court).

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil service competence and spoils system
rubrics_metrics.description: The subordinate civil service of a State is small but increasing; legislatures are not always alive to securing high competence, and the 'Spoils System' too often makes places the reward for electioneering and wire-pulling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms mirroring Federal civil service reforms are being introduced in some States (e.g., New York) to protect parts of the civil service from politics and secure competent men; such reforms would not apply to the higher elected officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment procedures for executive officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Every State provides for the impeachment of executive officers for grave offences; the State House of Representatives is the impeaching body (except Nebraska), and the State Senate sits as the tribunal, two-thirds majority generally required for conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impeachments are rare in practice; procedural variations exist (Nebraska uses joint resolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal and suspension of officials
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been a power in many States of removing officials, sometimes by vote of the legislature, sometimes by the governor on the address of both houses, or by the governor alone or with concurrence of the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removals must be for some offence or sufficient cause, not caprice or party motives; when immediate removal seems unjustified the governor may be empowered to suspend the officer pending investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recall of public officials
rubrics_metrics.description: A prescribed number of voting citizens may demand that a vote be taken on whether a certain official shall or shall not continue in office for the rest of his term; a majority against the official dismisses him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Up to the end of 1913 seven states had adopted this plan: Oregon, California, Arizona, Colorado, Nevada, Idaho, Washington.

rubrics_metrics.name: State judiciary structure (three sets of courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judiciary in every State includes three sets of courts: a Supreme court or court of appeal; superior courts of record; local courts; particular names and arrangements vary greatly from State to State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various historic English court names survive (common pleas, probate, surrogate, oyer and terminer, etc.); arrangements for criminal business vary and some States provide tribunals of arbitration and conciliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law and equity distinction or fusion
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been great diversity: some States once possessed separate courts of chancery; in several States there has been a complete fusion of law and equity; in others equity is administered by same judges or special chancery courts remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seven States (Connecticut, New York, North Carolina, Georgia, Ohio, California, and Idaho) have complete fusion; special chancery courts survive chiefly in older Eastern or Southern States; fusion choices affect procedure and judicial discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional limits and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The jurisdiction of the State courts, both civil and criminal, is absolutely unlimited except in certain cases specified by the Federal Constitution where some point of Federal law arises; certain classes of cases are reserved for Federal courts and in some the State courts enjoy concurrent jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All crimes (except those punishable under Federal statute) are justiciable by State courts; State systems often allow wider facilities for setting aside jury verdicts by raising legal points than European countries, a facility sometimes abused to community detriment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full faith and comity between States (recognition and extradition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State recognizes the judgments of the courts of a sister State, gives credit to its public acts and records, and delivers up to its justice any fugitive from its jurisdiction, permitting him to be tried for other offences than that in respect of which extradition was obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts of one State are not bound to follow the reported decisions of another State but use them for enlightenment and as evidence of common law; this comity facilitates inter-state relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision, codification, and codes of procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Most States have made sweeping changes in their judicial system and the form of their law: they have revised and codified statutes, adopted codes of procedure, and in some enacted codes embodying common law fused with statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codification is popular with the public for perceived simplicity and cheaper, speedier justice, but has been generally condemned by the abler profession as rendering law more uncertain and less scientific; codification may increase legal divergence between States (Louisiana as exception due to civil law basis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on judges' powers and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers of a judge are limited by State Constitutions: he is not generally allowed to charge the jury on questions of fact, but only to state the law; sometimes required to put his charge in writing; contempt power often restricted; forbidden to sit in causes with family or pecuniary interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some Constitutions enforce punctual attendance (e.g., provision that attorneys may agree on a substitute if judge not present within half an hour); California and Idaho have provisions requiring judges to decide causes within set timeframes or withhold salary until decisions are made; these limitations vary by State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of appointing judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods vary: historically appointment by Governor, election by legislature, or election by the people; in the period between 1812 and 1860 many States moved to popular election of judges, and at present some States have legislative election, some gubernatorial appointment with confirmation, and the rest popular election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four States elect judges by the legislature; seven appoint by Governor subject to confirmation; in all other States judges are elected by the people (including nearly all Western and Southwestern States and New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio); democratization trends and regional patterns are significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure of judicial office
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally superior judges were appointed for life during good behaviour; the wave of democracy has swept away life-tenure in nearly all States — only three now retain it — and judges are elected or appointed for terms varying from two to twenty-one years, with re-eligibility common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removal on address by legislature (majority of two-thirds in each house usually required) remains a safeguard; average term is eight to ten years; re-election is likely if judge gives satisfaction to bar and party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial salaries and related practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The book notes remarkable changes in judicial salaries and 'strange practice' prevailing in this matter, implying salaries are subject to political influence and varied provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include California's withholding of salary until judge certifies no causes undecided for ninety days; other States have different attendance and salary-related provisions; salary practices can be used to enforce judicial performance or create pressure.
